blurb: Reconnaissance, scanning, the OWASP Top 10, privilege escalation, and an honest introduction to reverse engineering and binary exploitation.

adaptedFrom.name: Awesome Cyber Security University
adaptedFrom.note: Module sequencing follows the CC0 red-team roadmap. Objectives, teaching notes, and framing are written by Sikhi University. No lab content is rehosted — every lab opens on the platform that runs it.

modules.title: Authorisation first
modules.objective: State, for any test you run, who authorised it, what is in scope, and what you will do if you find something you were not looking for.
modules.teach: Every technique in this path is legal in a lab and a criminal offence against a system you were not given. That is not a disclaimer we are appending; it is the first thing a professional learns, and the thing that separates this path from the thing it superficially resembles. Read the engagement material before the tooling. If a module ever tempts you to try something "just to see" against a system you do not own — that is the moment the training was for.

modules.title: Reconnaissance and scanning
modules.objective: Enumerate a target's hosts, ports, services, and subdomains, and read a scan result rather than merely producing one.
modules.teach: Beginners run a scanner and paste the output. Practitioners run a scanner and know which three lines matter. Learn the multiplexer first so long-running scans survive a dropped connection, then work through host discovery, service and version detection, and subdomain enumeration. Time spent here is repaid at every later stage: almost every successful engagement is won during enumeration.

modules.title: The exploitation toolchain
modules.objective: Use Metasploit and Hydra deliberately — knowing what each module does before you fire it — and get an initial foothold on a practice box.
modules.teach: A framework is a force multiplier for someone who already understands the attack and a liability for someone who does not. Read each module's source before you run it: you are executing someone else's code against a target, and on a real engagement you will be asked what it did. Credential attacks come with a matching lesson in defence — every failed login you generate is a detection someone else should be writing.

modules.title: Hashes, encodings, and where they leak
modules.objective: Identify a hash by its shape, crack a weak one, and explain why salting and a slow algorithm defeat you.
modules.teach: Cracking is the part of offence that teaches the most defence. Once you have watched an unsalted MD5 list fall in seconds and a properly salted, slow hash refuse to move at all, password storage stops being an abstract recommendation. Steganography and file-carving sit alongside it here because in practice the credential is rarely where you expected it to be.

modules.title: The web — OWASP Top 10 in practice
modules.objective: Find and exploit injection, broken access control, and file-inclusion flaws in a deliberately vulnerable application, then describe the fix.
modules.teach: Most of what gets breached is a web application, which makes this the highest-value module in the path. Work the Top 10 as a checklist first, then take Juice Shop apart at your own pace — it contains a graded challenge for nearly every category. Finish each finding the way a report does: the request that proved it, the impact, and the one-line change that closes it.

modules.title: Privilege escalation
modules.objective: Turn a low-privilege shell into administrative access on both Linux and Windows, using misconfiguration before exploitation.
modules.teach: Getting a shell is rarely the end of the assessment; it is the beginning of the interesting half. Most escalation is not an exploit at all but a misconfiguration — a writable service binary, an over-permissive sudo rule, a scheduled task running as SYSTEM. Learn to enumerate first and reach for a kernel exploit last, which is also the order that will not crash your client's production host.

modules.title: Reverse engineering and binary exploitation
modules.objective: Open a compiled binary in a disassembler, follow its logic, and understand how a buffer overflow becomes control of execution.
modules.teach: This is the deepest and slowest module in the path, and the one that pays off for the longest. Assembly and a disassembler let you answer questions about software nobody gave you the source to — which is most malware, most firmware, and a good deal of commercial code. Expect this to take considerably longer than the modules before it. That is the correct experience, not a sign you have gone wrong.
